title: Surface anatomy of the thorax
summary: Count ribs from the sternal angle, then draw the pleura, lungs and heart on the skin.
objectives: Find the sternal angle and list what lies at its level
Use the vertical reference lines to place the apex beat and a chest drain
Draw the pleural and lung margins on the chest wall
Mark the heart borders and the four auscultation areas
Use scapular landmarks to count levels on the back
takeaways: The sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage and the T4/5 plane.
Pleura: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Lungs: two ribs higher laterally — 6, 8, 10.
The apex beat is in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line.
A chest drain goes in the triangle of safety, just above a rib.
Auscultation areas are where the sound carries, not where the valves lie.

steps.title: Start at the sternal angle
steps.text:
Run a finger down from the jugular notch: the first ridge you meet is the sternal angle, the joint between manubrium and body. The second costal cartilage joins here, so it is the place to start counting ribs — the first rib is hidden behind the clavicle.

A horizontal plane through the sternal angle passes back to the T4/5 disc. At this level the aortic arch begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates, the azygos arches into the SVC, and the superior mediastinum meets the inferior.

check.q: Which costal cartilage joins the sternum at the sternal angle, and which vertebral level is opposite?
check.a: The second; the T4/5 intervertebral disc.

steps.title: The vertical lines and the triangle of safety
steps.text:
Vertical reference lines give the other coordinate: the midclavicular line through the midpoint of the clavicle, and the anterior and posterior axillary lines along the folds of the axilla, with the midaxillary line between them. The apex beat is normally in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

A chest drain goes in the triangle of safety: bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, and a line at the level of the fifth intercostal space, with its apex below the axilla.
steps.clinical: A displaced apex beat — lateral or lower than the fifth space in the midclavicular line — suggests cardiac enlargement or mediastinal shift.

check.q: Why is a chest drain inserted just above a rib rather than just below one?
check.a: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib.

steps.title: Where the pleura and lungs reach
steps.text: The parietal pleura starts above the medial clavicle, meets its fellow behind the sternum at the second cartilage, and follows a simple sequence round the chest: the left side diverges at 4 for the heart, then 6 in the midclavicular line, 8 in the midaxillary line, 10 in the scapular line and 12 beside the spine. The lungs follow the same course two ribs higher from the midclavicular line back — 6, 8, 10 — leaving a costodiaphragmatic recess of pleura below them.
steps.clinical: The pleura extends below the 12th rib medially, where it can be opened in a posterior approach to the kidney. The oblique fissure runs from about the T3 spinous process to the sixth costal cartilage — roughly the line of the medial border of the scapula with the arm raised.

check.q: At which rib does the lower margin of the pleura cross the midaxillary line?
check.a: The 8th rib.

steps.title: The heart on the chest wall
steps.text:
The heart's outline joins four points: the second left costal cartilage a finger's breadth from the sternum, the third right cartilage close to the sternum, the sixth right cartilage, and the apex in the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

Valve sounds are heard best where the blood carries them: aortic — right second intercostal space; pulmonary — left second space; tricuspid — left lower sternal edge; mitral — the apex.
steps.pitfall: The auscultation areas are not the surface positions of the valves; all four valves lie close together behind the sternum.

check.q: Where is the mitral valve best heard?
check.a: At the apex — left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line — not over the valve itself, which lies behind the left half of the sternum at the fourth cartilage.

steps.title: Counting on the back
steps.text:
With the arms by the side, the spine of the scapula lies at the level of the T3 spinous process and the inferior angle at T7. The vertebra prominens (C7) is the first spinous process that stands out at the base of the neck.

Between trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula lies the triangle of auscultation, where only thin muscle covers the chest wall.
steps.clinical: Pleural fluid is usually tapped posteriorly, one or two spaces below the top of the dullness, in the scapular or posterior axillary line and above the ninth rib to keep clear of the diaphragm and the organs beneath it.

check.q: Which spinous process lies level with the inferior angle of the scapula?

title: Surface anatomy of the abdomen
summary: Nine regions, four planes and a handful of points that tell you what lies beneath your hand.
objectives: Divide the abdomen into regions and quadrants
Locate the transpyloric plane and list the structures at its level
Place McBurney's point, Murphy's point and the umbilical landmarks
Describe how the liver, spleen and kidneys are examined
Distinguish an inguinal from a femoral hernia by the pubic tubercle
takeaways: Midclavicular lines plus the subcostal and intertubercular planes make nine regions.
The transpyloric plane (L1) crosses the pylorus, pancreatic neck, renal hila and gallbladder fundus.
The umbilicus lies at L3/4 and in the T10 dermatome; the aorta divides at L4.
McBurney's point is two thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine.
An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle, a femoral hernia below and lateral.

steps.title: Nine regions
steps.text:
Two vertical lines (the midclavicular lines, running down to the mid-inguinal points) and two horizontal planes (the subcostal plane at the lowest point of the costal margin and the intertubercular plane through the tubercles of the iliac crests) divide the abdomen into nine regions: the right and left hypochondriac, epigastric, right and left lateral (lumbar), umbilical, right and left inguinal (iliac) and hypogastric (suprapubic).

For quick clinical description, two lines through the umbilicus give four quadrants.

check.q: Which two horizontal planes define the nine abdominal regions?
check.a: The subcostal plane and the intertubercular plane.

steps.title: The transpyloric plane
steps.text: Halfway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis — or a hand's breadth below the xiphoid — lies the transpyloric plane, at the level of L1. It crosses the pylorus (in the supine patient), the neck of the pancreas, the hila of the kidneys, the duodenojejunal flexure and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery. Where it meets the right costal margin, at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, lies the fundus of the gallbladder. The adult spinal cord ends close to this level.
steps.clinical: Murphy's sign is elicited at the gallbladder point: the patient catches their breath on inspiration as an inflamed gallbladder descends onto the examining hand.

check.q: Name four structures at the level of the transpyloric plane.
check.a: Pylorus, neck of pancreas, renal hila, gallbladder fundus (also the duodenojejunal flexure, SMA origin and the end of the spinal cord).

steps.title: The umbilicus and the aorta
steps.text:
The umbilicus usually lies at the L3/4 disc, in the T10 dermatome. The abdominal aorta divides into the common iliac arteries at L4, just below and to the left of the umbilicus; the supracristal plane through the top of the iliac crests is at the L4 spinous process.

So a pulsation felt above the umbilicus is the aorta; a wide, expansile one is an aneurysm.
steps.clinical: Periumbilical pain is T10 — the referred pain of the midgut, which is why early appendicitis hurts around the umbilicus before localising to the right iliac fossa.

check.q: At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate?

steps.title: McBurney's point
steps.text: Two thirds of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine lies McBurney's point, the surface marking of the base of the appendix. The base is constant — where the three taeniae coli meet on the caecum — but the tip can point in any direction, retrocaecal most often.
steps.pitfall: A pelvic appendix may cause little abdominal tenderness but pain on rectal examination, diarrhoea or urinary symptoms; a retrocaecal one may irritate psoas and hurt on hip extension.

check.q: Why does the site of pain in appendicitis vary between patients?
check.a: The base is fixed, but the tip may be retrocaecal, pelvic, subcaecal or pre- or post-ileal, irritating different structures.

steps.title: Liver, spleen and kidneys
steps.text: The liver lies under the right costal margin; its lower edge descends with inspiration and is palpated from the right iliac fossa upward as the patient breathes in. The spleen lies under the left 9th–11th ribs along the 10th, behind the midaxillary line; it must be about three times its normal size to be felt, and it enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, with a notch on its front edge and no palpable upper border. The kidneys are felt bimanually, moving with respiration and ballotable.

check.q: How can you tell an enlarged spleen from an enlarged left kidney?
check.a: The spleen enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, has a notch, you cannot get above it, it is dull to percussion and not ballotable; the kidney is ballotable with a resonant band of colon in front.

steps.title: Hernias and the pubic tubercle
steps.text:
The inguinal ligament runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The femoral artery is at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis; the deep inguinal ring is above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic tubercle.

An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia below and lateral to it.
steps.clinical: Femoral hernias are commoner in women, have a narrow neck bounded by the lacunar ligament, and strangulate readily — they should be repaired promptly.

check.q: Where does a femoral hernia lie relative to the pubic tubercle?
check.a: Below and lateral to it (an inguinal hernia is above and medial).

title: Pulses, venous access and injection sites
summary: Where to feel, where to put a needle, and what to avoid on the way.
objectives: Locate the pulses of the upper limb, lower limb and neck
Describe the veins used for venepuncture and cannulation and what lies beneath them
Explain the purpose of the Allen test
Locate the great saphenous vein at the ankle and groin
Choose intramuscular injection sites that avoid the axillary and sciatic nerves
takeaways: Radial pulse: lateral to flexor carpi radialis. Brachial: medial to the biceps tendon.
Femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point; dorsalis pedis lateral to extensor hallucis longus; posterior tibial behind the medial malleolus.
The median cubital vein lies on the bicipital aponeurosis, which shields the brachial artery and median nerve.
The great saphenous vein runs just in front of the medial malleolus — constant enough for a cut-down.
Inject the deltoid in its upper part and the buttock in the upper outer quadrant.

steps.title: Upper limb pulses
steps.text: The radial pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, where the artery lies on the distal radius. The brachial pulse is in the cubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon — this is where the stethoscope goes when you take a blood pressure. The ulnar pulse is fainter, lateral to flexor carpi ulnaris.
steps.clinical: Arterial blood gases are usually taken from the radial artery because it is superficial, lies over bone for compression and has collateral supply through the palmar arches.

check.q: What is the Allen test for?
check.a: Before cannulating or sampling the radial artery, to confirm the ulnar artery alone can perfuse the hand through the palmar arches.

steps.title: Veins at the elbow
steps.text: The cephalic vein runs up the lateral side of the forearm and arm into the deltopectoral groove; the basilic vein runs up the medial side and pierces the deep fascia in the middle of the arm. The median cubital vein links them across the cubital fossa, lying on the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve beneath.
steps.clinical: The cephalic vein at the wrist ('houseman's vein') is a reliable cannulation site; the superficial branch of the radial nerve crosses it and can be irritated by the needle.

check.q: What protects the brachial artery during venepuncture of the median cubital vein?
check.a: The bicipital aponeurosis, which lies between the vein and the artery with the median nerve.

steps.title: Head and neck
steps.text:
The carotid pulse is felt at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, where the common carotid divides. The superficial temporal pulse is just in front of the tragus, and the facial pulse where the artery crosses the lower border of the mandible at the front of masseter.

The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the carotid in the carotid sheath; the external jugular vein crosses sternocleidomastoid superficially and is visible when venous pressure is raised.

check.q: Why should carotid sinus massage be done on one side only, and with care?
check.a: The sinus is a baroreceptor at the bifurcation; pressing it slows the heart and lowers blood pressure, and pressing both can cause asystole or syncope — and it can dislodge plaque.

steps.title: Lower limb pulses
steps.text: The femoral pulse is at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, with the femoral vein medial and the nerve lateral. The popliteal pulse is deep and felt with both hands with the knee slightly flexed. The posterior tibial pulse lies behind the medial malleolus, halfway to the heel. The dorsalis pedis pulse lies on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
steps.mnemonic: NAVY from lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts.
steps.clinical: Absent foot pulses with a cold, pale foot point to peripheral arterial disease; the dorsalis pedis is congenitally absent in a small proportion of people, so always check both foot pulses.

check.q: From lateral to medial, what lies in the femoral triangle at the inguinal ligament?
check.a: Nerve, artery, vein, then the empty space of the femoral canal (with lymphatics).

steps.title: The great saphenous vein
steps.text: The great saphenous vein begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch, passes just in front of the medial malleolus — the most constant vein in the body — and runs up the medial leg and thigh with the saphenous nerve below the knee. It joins the femoral vein at the saphenous opening, 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
steps.clinical: Its valves fail in varicose veins, most often at the saphenofemoral junction. It is the commonest conduit for coronary artery bypass grafting, reversed so its valves do not block flow. Stripping it can injure the saphenous nerve and numb the medial leg.

check.q: Where can the great saphenous vein always be found, even in a collapsed patient?
check.a: Just anterior to the medial malleolus.

steps.title: Where to give an intramuscular injection
steps.text:
The deltoid is used for small volumes. Inject into its upper part, about three fingers below the acromion: the axillary nerve runs horizontally around the humerus about 5–6 cm below the acromion.

In the buttock, inject into the upper outer quadrant, or better the ventrogluteal site in gluteus medius, well away from the sciatic nerve, which emerges below piriformis in the lower medial part. In infants, vastus lateralis is used.
steps.clinical: A misplaced gluteal injection can cause sciatic nerve injury, usually affecting the common fibular division most: a foot drop.

check.q: Why should a gluteal injection be given in the upper outer quadrant?
check.a: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner part of the buttock; the upper outer quadrant is clear of it.

title: The axilla
summary: A pyramid of muscle through which every vessel, nerve and lymphatic of the upper limb must pass.
objectives: Describe the apex, base and four walls of the axilla
Divide the axillary artery into three parts and name the branches of each
Name the nerves at risk in axillary surgery and the deficit from each
Describe the axillary lymph node groups and surgical levels
Give the boundaries and contents of the quadrangular space
takeaways: Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor. Posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus. Medial: serratus anterior.
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts with one, two and three branches.
Long thoracic nerve: winged scapula. Thoracodorsal: weak latissimus. Intercostobrachial: numb inner arm.
Level I nodes lie below pectoralis minor, level II behind it, level III above it.
The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.

steps.title: A pyramid with four walls
steps.text: The axilla is a pyramid. Its apex, the cervico-axillary canal between clavicle, first rib and scapula, opens into the root of the neck. Its base is the skin and fascia of the armpit. The anterior wall is pectoralis major and minor; the posterior wall is subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi; the medial wall is serratus anterior over the upper ribs; and the lateral wall is the intertubercular groove of the humerus.

check.q: Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
check.a: Subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi.

steps.title: The axillary artery
steps.text: The subclavian artery becomes axillary at the outer border of the first rib and brachial at the lower border of teres major. Pectoralis minor crosses it and divides it into three parts with one, two and three branches: part 1 — superior thoracic; part 2 — thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic; part 3 — subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral.
steps.mnemonic: Screw The Lawyer, Save A Patient — superior thoracic, thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral.
steps.clinical: Branches of the subclavian (suprascapular, dorsal scapular) and of the subscapular artery anastomose round the scapula, so the axillary artery can be tied above the subscapular origin without losing the arm.

check.q: Which branches arise from the third part of the axillary artery?
check.a: The subscapular artery and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.

steps.title: Nerves on the walls
steps.text: The cords of the brachial plexus are named for their positions around the second part of the artery. Two nerves run on the walls and are at risk in axillary surgery: the long thoracic nerve on the surface of serratus anterior, and the thoracodorsal nerve with its vessels to latissimus dorsi. The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) crosses the axilla to the skin of the inner arm.
steps.clinical: The thoracodorsal pedicle is preserved when possible because latissimus dorsi is used as a flap in breast reconstruction. Numbness of the inner arm after node clearance is from division of the intercostobrachial nerve.

check.q: What happens if the long thoracic nerve is cut during axillary clearance?
check.a: Serratus anterior is paralysed: the medial border of the scapula wings when the patient pushes against a wall, and overhead abduction is weak.

steps.title: The axillary vein
steps.text: The axillary vein begins at the lower border of teres major as the continuation of the basilic vein, joined by the venae comitantes of the brachial artery, and receives the cephalic vein near its end. It lies medial to the artery and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
steps.clinical: Effort thrombosis (Paget–Schroetter syndrome) of the axillary–subclavian vein affects young athletes after repeated overhead activity, compressed between the first rib, clavicle and subclavius.

check.q: Where does the axillary vein lie relative to the artery?
check.a: Medial (and anterior) to it.

steps.title: The axillary nodes
steps.text:
About 20–30 nodes lie in five groups: anterior (pectoral) along the lateral thoracic vessels draining most of the breast; posterior (subscapular); lateral (humeral) along the vein draining the arm; central, in the fat of the axilla; and apical, at the apex, receiving from all the others and draining to the subclavian trunk.

Surgeons describe them by level relative to pectoralis minor: I below its lower border, II behind it, III above it.
steps.clinical: Removing many nodes interrupts the lymph drainage of the arm and can cause lifelong lymphoedema; sentinel node biopsy was introduced to avoid unnecessary clearance.

check.q: Which group of axillary nodes receives lymph from all the others?
check.a: The apical group.

steps.title: The quadrangular space
steps.text: Seen from behind, the posterior wall has gaps. The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor above, teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the surgical neck of the humerus laterally. Through it pass the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery, winding round the humerus to deltoid and teres minor.
steps.clinical: Anterior dislocation of the shoulder stretches the axillary nerve too; always document its function before and after reduction.

check.q: Which nerve is at risk in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, and how do you test it?
check.a: The axillary nerve — test sensation over the lower deltoid (the 'regimental badge' area) and deltoid contraction.

title: Nerve injuries of the upper limb
summary: Find the level of the lesion from which muscles still work and where the skin is numb.
objectives: Recognise upper and lower brachial plexus injuries
Distinguish radial nerve lesions in the axilla, spiral groove and forearm
Distinguish median nerve lesions at the elbow, in the forearm and at the wrist
Explain the ulnar paradox and Froment's sign
Use the autonomous sensory zones of the hand
takeaways: Erb (C5–6): waiter's tip. Klumpke (C8–T1): claw hand, sometimes with Horner syndrome.
Spiral groove radial lesion: wrist drop with triceps spared. Posterior interosseous: finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss.
Anterior interosseous lesion: cannot make an 'O' with thumb and index; no sensory loss.
A distal ulnar lesion claws more than a proximal one, because FDP to the ring and little fingers is spared.
Autonomous zones: index pulp — median; little finger pulp — ulnar; first dorsal web — radial.

steps.title: Upper and lower plexus injuries
steps.text:
Forcing the head away from the shoulder (a fall from a motorbike, a difficult delivery) tears the upper trunk (C5–6): Erb palsy. Deltoid, the rotator cuff, biceps and brachialis are lost, and the arm hangs adducted, medially rotated and extended at the elbow with the forearm pronated — the waiter's tip.

Forcing the arm up above the head (grabbing a branch while falling, a breech delivery) tears the lower trunk (C8–T1): Klumpke palsy, with paralysis of the small muscles of the hand, a claw hand and sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm.

check.q: Why may a Klumpke palsy be accompanied by a Horner syndrome?
check.a: The T1 root carries the preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head; a root avulsion at T1 interrupts them.

steps.title: The radial nerve at three levels
steps.text:
In the axilla (crutch palsy) all radial muscles are lost including triceps. In the spiral groove (midshaft humeral fracture, 'Saturday night palsy') triceps is largely spared because its branches arise higher, but the wrist and finger extensors and brachioradialis are lost: wrist drop, with numbness over the first dorsal web.

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch) can be trapped at supinator: the fingers and thumb drop but the wrist still extends — with radial deviation — because extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied before the division. There is no sensory loss.

check.q: A patient can extend the wrist (with radial deviation) but not the fingers, and has no numbness. Where is the lesion?
check.a: The posterior interosseous nerve — ECRL (supplied proximally) still works and the superficial sensory branch is intact.

steps.title: The median nerve at three levels
steps.text:
At the elbow (supracondylar fracture in a child) the long flexors to the thumb, index and middle fingers are lost: asked to make a fist, the index and middle fingers stay straight — the hand of benediction — and the thenar muscles and lateral palm lose function and sensation.

The anterior interosseous nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Its lesion stops the patient making an 'O' — the tip of the thumb and index collapse into a pinch — with no sensory loss.

At the wrist (carpal tunnel, a laceration) only the thenar muscles, lateral lumbricals and digital sensation are lost.

check.q: Why does an anterior interosseous nerve lesion cause no sensory loss?
check.a: The anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor (apart from joint branches).

steps.title: The ulnar nerve and its paradox
steps.text:
At the elbow, behind the medial epicondyle and in the cubital tunnel, the nerve is often compressed. At the wrist it can be damaged in Guyon's canal or by a laceration. Either way most of the intrinsic muscles are lost: the ring and little fingers claw (extended at the MCP joints, flexed at the IP joints) because their lumbricals and interossei are weak.

The paradox: the claw is worse in a wrist lesion, because flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers, supplied at the elbow, still works and pulls the fingers into flexion.
steps.clinical: The dorsal cutaneous branch leaves the ulnar nerve above the wrist, so sensation on the back of the ulnar hand is spared in a wrist lesion and lost in an elbow lesion — another way to tell the level.

check.q: What does Froment's sign test?
check.a: Adductor pollicis (ulnar): pinching paper between thumb and index, the patient flexes the thumb IP joint with flexor pollicis longus (median) to compensate.

steps.title: Nerves of the scapula
steps.text: The long thoracic nerve (C5–7) supplies serratus anterior; injury causes medial winging of the scapula. The accessory nerve supplies trapezius; injury causes a drooping shoulder and lateral winging. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and can be trapped at the suprascapular notch, giving weak initiation of abduction and lateral rotation with wasting above and below the spine of the scapula.

check.q: A patient's scapula wings medially when pushing against a wall. Which nerve is injured?
check.a: The long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior).

steps.title: Sensory maps and autonomous zones
steps.text:
On the palm the median nerve supplies the lateral three and a half digits (including their dorsal tips) and the lateral palm; the ulnar nerve the medial one and a half digits. On the dorsum the radial nerve supplies the lateral hand and the ulnar nerve the medial side.

Because territories overlap, test the autonomous zones supplied by one nerve alone: the pulp of the index finger (median), the pulp of the little finger (ulnar) and the skin of the first dorsal web space (radial).
focus: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve

check.q: Which area of skin tests the radial nerve most reliably?
check.a: The dorsum of the first web space.

title: Nerve injuries of the lower limb
summary: Foot drop, Trendelenburg and a numb thigh — which nerve, and is it the nerve or the root?
objectives: Recognise a common fibular nerve palsy and distinguish it from an L5 root lesion
Distinguish deep and superficial fibular nerve lesions
Explain the Trendelenburg sign and which side drops
Describe femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve lesions
Explain why a sciatic nerve injury often behaves like a fibular nerve injury
takeaways: The common fibular nerve winds round the neck of the fibula, just under the skin.
Foot drop with preserved inversion suggests the fibular nerve; weak inversion and hip abduction as well suggest L5.
In a Trendelenburg sign the pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg; the weak muscles are on the stance side.
Femoral lesion: weak knee extension and absent knee jerk. Meralgia paraesthetica: numb lateral thigh, no weakness.
The fibular division of the sciatic nerve is more easily injured than the tibial.

steps.title: Foot drop at the fibular neck
steps.text:
The common fibular nerve leaves the popliteal fossa along biceps femoris and winds round the neck of the fibula, lying on bone just under the skin, before dividing. It is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb: a tight plaster, a fibular neck fracture, prolonged crossing of the legs or lying unconscious on a hard surface.

The result is foot drop (lost dorsiflexion and toe extension), lost eversion, a high-stepping gait and numbness of the dorsum of the foot and lower lateral leg.

check.q: A patient has foot drop but can invert the foot strongly. Nerve or L5 root?
check.a: The common fibular nerve — inversion by tibialis posterior (tibial nerve, L5) is preserved; an L5 root lesion would weaken inversion and hip abduction too.

steps.title: Deep or superficial fibular
steps.text: The deep fibular nerve enters the anterior compartment and supplies the dorsiflexors — tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis tertius — and ends as a small sensory branch to the first web space. The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis (eversion) and then most of the skin of the dorsum of the foot.

check.q: What is often the first sign of an anterior compartment syndrome?
check.a: Numbness of the first dorsal web space, from pressure on the deep fibular nerve — along with pain on passive stretch of the toes.

steps.title: The sciatic nerve
steps.text: The sciatic nerve is really two nerves in one sheath: a tibial division and a common fibular division, which separate at a variable level above the knee. The fibular division lies laterally, has fewer fascicles and less connective tissue, and is tethered at the fibular neck — so it is damaged more easily by stretch or pressure.
steps.clinical: Sciatic injury follows posterior hip dislocation, acetabular fracture, hip replacement and misplaced gluteal injections.

check.q: Why does a posterior dislocation of the hip often cause a foot drop rather than a complete sciatic palsy?
check.a: The femoral head is driven back against the sciatic nerve, and the fibular division is more vulnerable, so its territory suffers most.

steps.title: The Trendelenburg sign
steps.text: When you stand on one leg, gluteus medius and minimus of the stance leg contract to hold the pelvis level against the weight of the lifted side. Both are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. If they are weak, the pelvis sags on the side of the lifted leg, and the patient lurches the trunk over the stance leg while walking.
steps.pitfall: The pelvis drops on the sound side. The lesion is on the side the patient is standing on.

check.q: A patient stands on the right leg and the left side of the pelvis drops. Which side is weak?
check.a: The right — the right gluteus medius and minimus (right superior gluteal nerve) cannot hold the pelvis.

steps.title: The femoral nerve
steps.text: The femoral nerve (L2–4) supplies quadriceps and the skin of the front of the thigh, and continues as the saphenous nerve to the medial leg and foot. A lesion — from a psoas haematoma, pelvic surgery or femoral catheterisation — weakens knee extension so the knee buckles, abolishes the knee jerk, and numbs the anterior thigh and medial leg.

check.q: How can you tell a femoral nerve lesion from an L4 root lesion?
check.a: In an L4 root lesion hip adduction (obturator nerve, also L2–4) and often tibialis anterior are weak too; in a femoral nerve lesion they are normal.

steps.title: Obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves
steps.text:
The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal to the adductors and a patch of skin on the medial thigh; it can be compressed during labour or damaged in pelvic surgery, weakening adduction.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory. It passes under or through the inguinal ligament close to the ASIS, where it can be compressed by a tight belt, obesity or pregnancy: meralgia paraesthetica, burning numbness of the lateral thigh with no weakness and normal reflexes.

check.q: A pregnant woman has burning numbness of the outer thigh, normal power and normal reflexes. What is the diagnosis?
check.a: Meralgia paraesthetica — compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at the inguinal ligament.

title: The ankle: retinacula and the tarsal tunnel
summary: Everything that crosses the ankle is strapped down — learn the order and you can find each one by touch.
objectives: Name the retinacula of the ankle
List in order the structures behind the medial malleolus
List in order the structures crossing the front of the ankle
Describe the fibular tendons and their retinacula
Name the ligaments injured in an inversion sprain
takeaways: Behind the medial malleolus: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, artery and veins, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.
In front: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, dorsalis pedis artery, deep fibular nerve, extensor digitorum longus.
Tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum.
The fibular tendons share a sheath behind the lateral malleolus under the superior fibular retinaculum.
An inversion sprain tears the anterior talofibular ligament first.

steps.title: Five straps
steps.text: Tendons crossing the ankle would bowstring when the muscles contract if they were not held down. In front, the superior extensor retinaculum passes between tibia and fibula above the joint, and the Y-shaped inferior extensor retinaculum loops over the tendons on the dorsum. Medially the flexor retinaculum runs from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus. Laterally the superior and inferior fibular retinacula hold the fibular tendons.

check.q: Between which two bony points does the flexor retinaculum run?
check.a: The medial malleolus and the medial process of the calcaneus.

steps.title: The tarsal tunnel
steps.text: Under the flexor retinaculum, behind the medial malleolus, pass from front to back: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery with its venae comitantes, the tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus. Each tendon has its own synovial sheath.
steps.clinical: In tarsal tunnel syndrome the tibial nerve or its plantar branches are compressed here, giving burning pain and numbness of the sole, worse at night — the lower limb's carpal tunnel.

check.q: Name the contents of the tarsal tunnel from anterior to posterior.
check.a: Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery and veins, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.

steps.title: The front of the ankle
steps.text:
Under the extensor retinacula, from medial to lateral: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, the anterior tibial artery (becoming dorsalis pedis) with the deep fibular nerve, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius.

The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by asking the patient to lift the big toe and feeling just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.
steps.mnemonic: The Hospital's Awfully Nice During Parties — Tibialis anterior, Hallucis longus, Artery, Nerve, Digitorum longus, Peroneus (fibularis) tertius.

check.q: What lies immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum of the foot?
check.a: The dorsalis pedis artery with the deep fibular nerve.

steps.title: Behind the lateral malleolus
steps.text: Fibularis longus and brevis run behind the lateral malleolus in a common synovial sheath, held by the superior fibular retinaculum, then separate: brevis to the base of the fifth metatarsal, longus under the cuboid and across the sole to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal. The sural nerve and small saphenous vein pass behind the malleolus more superficially.
steps.clinical: A tear of the superior fibular retinaculum lets the tendons snap forward over the malleolus — painful recurrent subluxation after a skiing or football injury.
show: Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscles

check.q: Where does fibularis brevis insert, and what fracture can it cause?
check.a: The tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal; an avulsion fracture there in an inversion injury.

steps.title: The sprained ankle
steps.text: The lateral collateral ligament has three bands: the anterior talofibular, the calcaneofibular and the strong posterior talofibular. In the common plantarflexion–inversion injury the anterior talofibular ligament tears first, then the calcaneofibular. The medial (deltoid) ligament is so strong that eversion tends to avulse the medial malleolus rather than tear it.
steps.clinical: The Ottawa ankle rules — bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to bear weight — decide who needs an X-ray.

check.q: Which ligament is torn first in an inversion sprain?
check.a: The anterior talofibular ligament.

title: The palm: sheaths, spaces and the snuffbox
summary: Why an infected finger can end up in the palm, and why a tender snuffbox needs an X-ray.
objectives: Describe the palmar aponeurosis and Dupuytren's contracture
Describe the synovial sheaths of the flexor tendons and their connections
Recognise the signs of flexor tendon sheath infection
Explain the importance of flexor tendon zone II
Give the boundaries and floor of the anatomical snuffbox
takeaways: The palmar aponeurosis is continuous with palmaris longus and anchors the palmar skin.
The little finger sheath is continuous with the ulnar bursa, the thumb sheath with the radial bursa.
Kanavel's signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension.
Zone II, where both flexor tendons lie in the fibrous sheath, is where repairs most easily adhere.
Snuffbox tenderness after a fall means a scaphoid fracture until proved otherwise.

steps.title: The palmar aponeurosis
steps.text: Beneath the thick palmar skin lies a triangular sheet of dense fascia, the palmar aponeurosis, continuous with the tendon of palmaris longus at the wrist. It splits into four slips to the fingers and is tied to the skin by fibrous bands — the reason palmar skin does not slide when you grip.
steps.clinical: Dupuytren's disease is familial and commoner in men of northern European descent, with diabetes, alcohol excess and epilepsy. The patient cannot lay the hand flat on a table.

check.q: What is Dupuytren's contracture?
check.a: Nodular thickening and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, pulling the ring and little fingers into flexion at the MCP and PIP joints.

steps.title: Synovial sheaths and bursae
steps.text: In the fingers the flexor tendons run in a fibrous sheath lined by a synovial sheath. In the palm the eight tendons of FDS and FDP share one sheath, the ulnar bursa, and flexor pollicis longus has its own, the radial bursa. The ulnar bursa is continuous with the sheath of the little finger and the radial bursa with that of the thumb; the sheaths of the index, middle and ring fingers usually end at the level of the MCP joints.
focus: Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus

check.q: Why can an infection of the little finger sheath spread to the thumb?
check.a: The little finger sheath is continuous with the ulnar bursa, which often communicates with the radial bursa at the wrist — giving a 'horseshoe' abscess.

steps.title: Infections of the sheath and the pulp
steps.text:
A penetrating injury over a flexion crease can seed infection into a sheath. The finger is held slightly flexed, swollen along its whole length, tender along the sheath, and extremely painful on passive extension — Kanavel's signs. It is a surgical emergency: pus under pressure destroys the tendon's blood supply.

The pulp of the fingertip is divided into tight compartments by fibrous septa running from skin to bone, so a pulp infection (felon) is intensely painful and can threaten the distal phalanx.

check.q: Which of Kanavel's signs is said to be the most sensitive?
check.a: Pain on passive extension of the finger.

steps.title: Zone II — 'no man's land'
steps.text: Flexor tendon injuries are described by zone. In zone II, from the distal palmar crease to the insertion of FDS on the middle phalanx, both FDS and FDP run inside the tight fibrous sheath, and FDP passes through the split in FDS. Repairs here readily adhere to the sheath and to each other, and once had such poor results that the zone was called 'no man's land'.

check.q: How do you test flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis separately?
check.a: FDP: hold the middle phalanx and ask the patient to bend the fingertip. FDS: hold the other fingers straight and ask them to bend the finger at the PIP joint.

steps.title: The anatomical snuffbox
steps.text: With the thumb extended, a hollow appears on the radial side of the wrist. Its anterior (lateral) boundary is the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; its posterior (medial) boundary is the tendon of extensor pollicis longus. In its floor are the scaphoid and trapezium, and across it run the radial artery and, superficially, the cephalic vein and branches of the superficial radial nerve.
steps.clinical: Suspected scaphoid fractures are immobilised and re-imaged (or scanned by MRI) rather than dismissed.

check.q: Why is tenderness in the snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand taken seriously even if the X-ray is normal?
check.a: It suggests a scaphoid fracture, which may not show at first; the blood supply enters distally, so a missed waist fracture risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.

title: The vessels of the pelvis
summary: The internal iliac artery, its two divisions, and why a broken pelvis can empty the circulation.
objectives: Describe the common iliac bifurcation and the ureter's relation to it
Name the branches of the posterior and anterior divisions of the internal iliac artery
Follow the internal pudendal artery out of the pelvis and into the perineum
Explain the corona mortis
Explain the haemorrhage of pelvic fracture and the spread of cancer through the pelvic veins
takeaways: The common iliac divides in front of the sacroiliac joint, where the ureter crosses it.
Posterior division: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal — all parietal.
Anterior division: visceral branches plus obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal.
An obturator artery arising from the inferior epigastric crosses the superior pubic ramus — the corona mortis.
The pelvic veins communicate with the valveless vertebral venous plexus.

steps.title: The bifurcation and the ureter
steps.text:
The aorta divides at L4; each common iliac artery divides again in front of the sacroiliac joint. The external iliac follows the pelvic brim to the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery. The internal iliac descends into the pelvis towards the upper border of the greater sciatic notch and divides into anterior and posterior divisions.

The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.
steps.clinical: The ureter is at risk wherever pelvic vessels are tied — at the pelvic brim and, in women, where the uterine artery crosses above it ('water under the bridge').

check.q: Where does the ureter enter the pelvis?
check.a: Over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, in front of the sacroiliac joint.

steps.title: The posterior division
steps.text: The posterior division supplies the body wall only. It gives the iliolumbar artery (iliacus and the lumbar region), the lateral sacral arteries (to the sacral canal) and the large superior gluteal artery, which leaves through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve to supply gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae.
steps.mnemonic: I L S — the posterior division gives Iliolumbar, Lateral sacral, Superior gluteal.
steps.clinical: The superior gluteal artery lies on the bone at the greater sciatic notch and can be torn in fractures through it.
focus: Posterior division of internal iliac artery

check.q: Name the three branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.
check.a: Iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal.

steps.title: The anterior division
steps.text:
The anterior division supplies the viscera and some parietal territory. The umbilical artery gives the superior vesical arteries (its distal part becoming the medial umbilical ligament); the inferior vesical (or vaginal and uterine in women) and middle rectal arteries supply the bladder, prostate or uterus and rectum. The obturator artery runs to the obturator canal. The inferior gluteal and internal pudendal arteries leave through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.

The internal pudendal artery then hooks round the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal with the pudendal nerve, to supply the perineum.
focus: Anterior division of internal iliac artery

check.q: By which route does the internal pudendal artery reach the perineum?
check.a: Out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, round the ischial spine, then in through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.

steps.title: The corona mortis
steps.text: The obturator artery usually arises from the anterior division. In about a quarter of people an accessory or replaced obturator artery arises instead from the inferior epigastric (and so from the external iliac) and descends over the superior pubic ramus, close to the lacunar ligament and the femoral ring.

check.q: Why is an aberrant obturator artery called the 'crown of death'?
check.a: It crosses the superior pubic ramus next to the femoral ring, where it can be cut when incising the lacunar ligament to free a femoral hernia or torn in a pubic fracture, causing brisk bleeding.

steps.title: Bleeding from a broken pelvis
steps.text: A pelvic ring fracture can bleed several litres into the retroperitoneum — mostly from the pelvic venous plexuses and fracture surfaces, and sometimes from branches of the internal iliac artery. First aid is mechanical: a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters closes the ring and reduces the volume. Arterial bleeding is stopped by angiographic embolisation of internal iliac branches; the rich collateral circulation of the pelvis keeps the viscera alive.

check.q: Why can the internal iliac arteries be embolised without killing the pelvic organs?
check.a: There are extensive collaterals across the midline and from the lumbar, median sacral, inferior mesenteric and femoral systems.

steps.title: Veins that reach the spine
steps.text: The internal iliac veins receive the pelvic venous plexuses — vesical, prostatic, rectal, uterine — and join the external iliac veins to form the common iliacs. The pelvic plexuses also communicate freely, without valves, with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson's plexus), especially when abdominal pressure rises.

check.q: Why does prostate cancer so often spread to the lumbar spine?
check.a: Prostatic veins communicate with the valveless vertebral venous plexus, which carries tumour cells directly to the vertebrae.

title: The posterior mediastinum
summary: Behind the heart: the oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos veins, thoracic duct and the sympathetic chains.
objectives: List the contents of the posterior mediastinum
Describe the relations and constrictions of the thoracic oesophagus
Describe the descending thoracic aorta and the blood supply of the spinal cord
Describe the azygos system and its role as a collateral pathway
Trace the thoracic duct and the splanchnic nerves
takeaways: Oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos and hemiazygos veins, thoracic duct, vagi; the sympathetic trunks lie just lateral.
The oesophagus is narrowed at the cricoid, the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and the diaphragm.
The great radicular artery (of Adamkiewicz) is at risk in thoracoabdominal aortic surgery.
The azygos arches over the right lung root into the SVC at T4.
The thoracic duct crosses from right to left at about T5 and ends at the left venous angle.

steps.title: What lies behind the heart
steps.text: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and in front of the bodies of T5–T12. It contains the oesophagus with the vagal plexus, the descending thoracic aorta, the azygos and hemiazygos veins, the thoracic duct and lymph nodes. The sympathetic trunks lie on the heads of the ribs just lateral to it.

check.q: Name the contents of the posterior mediastinum.
check.a: Oesophagus and vagi, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct and nodes (with the sympathetic trunks alongside).

steps.title: The thoracic oesophagus
steps.text: The oesophagus descends behind the trachea, the left main bronchus and the left atrium, drifting to the left to pass through the diaphragm at T10. It is narrowed in three places — at its start behind the cricoid (15 cm from the incisors), where it is crossed by the aortic arch and left main bronchus (about 25 cm), and at the diaphragm (about 40 cm).
steps.clinical: Swallowed tablets and foreign bodies lodge at the constrictions. The left atrium lies directly in front, which is why transoesophageal echocardiography sees it so well and a large left atrium can indent the barium-filled oesophagus.

check.q: Where are the three constrictions of the oesophagus?
check.a: At the cricopharyngeus (C6), where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross it, and at the diaphragmatic hiatus (T10).

steps.title: The descending aorta
steps.text:
The descending aorta begins at T4 and lies to the left of the vertebral bodies, passing behind the diaphragm through the aortic hiatus at T12. It gives posterior intercostal arteries to spaces 3–11, bronchial and oesophageal branches, and subcostal arteries.

Some intercostal and lumbar arteries feed the spinal cord through radicular arteries; the largest, the great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz, usually arises on the left between T9 and L2 and supplies the lower two thirds of the anterior spinal artery.

check.q: Why can repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm cause paraplegia?
check.a: The great radicular artery, on which the lower anterior spinal artery depends, may be excluded or clamped, infarcting the anterior cord.

steps.title: The azygos system
steps.text:
The azygos vein ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies, collecting the right posterior intercostal veins, and arches forward over the root of the right lung at T4 to enter the superior vena cava. On the left the hemiazygos (below) and accessory hemiazygos (above) veins drain the left intercostal spaces and cross behind the aorta to join it.

Below, the system connects with the lumbar veins and the IVC.
steps.clinical: When the IVC or SVC is blocked, the azygos system becomes a major collateral route back to the heart. On a chest film an enlarged azygos shadow at the right tracheobronchial angle suggests raised venous pressure.

check.q: Where does the azygos vein end?
check.a: In the superior vena cava, after arching over the root of the right lung at the level of T4.

steps.title: The thoracic duct
steps.text: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli near L1–2, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus, and ascends between the aorta and the azygos vein behind the oesophagus. At about T5 it crosses to the left, climbs behind the left side of the oesophagus into the neck, arches in front of the vertebral artery and ends at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.
steps.clinical: Chylothorax follows oesophagectomy and other thoracic surgery or lymphoma; the fluid is milky with a high triglyceride content.

check.q: A duct injury below T5 gives a chylothorax on which side, and above T5 on which side?
check.a: Below T5 usually the right; above T5 usually the left — because the duct crosses at about T5.

steps.title: The sympathetic trunks and splanchnic nerves
steps.text: The sympathetic trunks run down on the heads of the ribs, with a ganglion at each level. The upper ganglia send fibres to the heart, lungs and oesophagus. From the lower ganglia arise the thoracic splanchnic nerves — greater (T5–9), lesser (T10–11) and least (T12) — which pierce the crura to reach the coeliac, aorticorenal and renal ganglia. They carry preganglionic fibres that synapse in the abdomen, and visceral pain fibres back.
steps.clinical: Thoracoscopic division of the upper sympathetic chain (T2–3) treats severe palmar hyperhidrosis; coeliac plexus block relieves the pain of pancreatic cancer by interrupting visceral afferents carried in the splanchnic nerves.

check.q: From which segments does the greater splanchnic nerve arise, and where does it relay?
check.a: T5–T9; in the coeliac ganglion.

title: Lymph drainage of the abdomen and pelvis
summary: Nodes follow arteries — which is why the testis drains to the aorta and the scrotum to the groin.
objectives: State the rule that predicts the drainage of abdominal and pelvic organs
Describe the gastric, colonic and pre-aortic node groups
Explain the drainage of the testis and why it differs from the scrotum
Describe the pelvic node groups and the drainage above and below the pectinate line
List what drains to the superficial inguinal nodes
takeaways: Lymph follows the arteries: unpaired gut arteries to pre-aortic nodes, paired arteries to lateral aortic nodes.
Gastric cancer may reach Virchow's node in the left supraclavicular fossa via the thoracic duct.
Colonic resection takes the mesentery and nodes up to the origin of the supplying artery.
The testis drains to para-aortic nodes at L1–2; the scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
Superficial inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, the abdominal wall below the umbilicus, the perineum and the anal canal below the pectinate line.

steps.title: Nodes follow arteries
steps.text: The organs of the abdomen drain along their arteries. The gut, supplied by the unpaired coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries, drains to pre-aortic nodes around those origins. Organs supplied by paired lateral branches — kidneys, adrenals, gonads — drain to lateral aortic (para-aortic) nodes. Both reach the lumbar and intestinal trunks, the cisterna chyli and the thoracic duct.

check.q: Where does lymph from the kidney drain?
check.a: To the lateral aortic (para-aortic) nodes at the renal artery origins.

steps.title: The stomach and the coeliac nodes
steps.text: The stomach drains in four directions, following its arteries along the curvatures: to the gastric and gastro-omental nodes, the pyloric nodes, and the splenic and pancreatic nodes — and all ultimately to the coeliac nodes. From there lymph rises through the thoracic duct to the left venous angle.
steps.clinical: Gastrectomy for cancer removes the stomach with its node stations along each artery (a D2 resection) because the nodes cannot be judged by eye.

check.q: What is Troisier's sign?
check.a: A palpable left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node from an abdominal cancer, classically gastric, spread up the thoracic duct.

steps.title: The colon: a chain towards the aorta
steps.text: Colonic lymph passes through four tiers: epicolic nodes on the wall, paracolic nodes along the marginal artery, intermediate nodes along the named colic arteries (ileocolic, right, middle and left colic, sigmoid) and central nodes at the origin of the superior or inferior mesenteric artery.

check.q: Why does a colectomy for cancer divide the supplying artery at its origin?
check.a: So that the whole chain of nodes along it, up to the central nodes, is removed with the mesentery (a high tie).

steps.title: Testis to the aorta, scrotum to the groin
steps.text: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and descends, taking its artery, veins and lymphatics with it. Its lymph therefore runs up the spermatic cord to the lateral aortic nodes at L1–2, near the origin of the testicular artery. The scrotal skin, by contrast, belongs to the perineum and drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
steps.clinical: A testicular tumour is removed through an inguinal incision, not through the scrotum: cutting the scrotum opens a new drainage route to the inguinal nodes.

check.q: A man with a testicular tumour has enlarged nodes. Where do you look first?
check.a: In the para-aortic region at L1–2 — not the groin.

steps.title: The pelvic nodes and the pectinate line
steps.text:
Pelvic organs drain to the internal iliac, external iliac and obturator nodes and on to the common iliac and aortic nodes. The prostate and bladder drain mainly to internal and external iliac and obturator nodes; the upper rectum along the superior rectal vessels to the inferior mesenteric nodes.

The anal canal is split by the pectinate line: above it lymph follows the rectal vessels to internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes; below it lymph goes to the superficial inguinal nodes.

check.q: A squamous cancer of the anal margin spreads first to which nodes?
check.a: The superficial inguinal nodes — the anal canal below the pectinate line drains there.

steps.title: The inguinal nodes
steps.text: The superficial inguinal nodes lie in a horizontal group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical group along the end of the great saphenous vein. Between them they drain the superficial lower limb, the abdominal wall below the umbilicus, the buttock, the perineum and external genitalia (except the testis and glans), and the anal canal below the pectinate line. They drain in turn to the deep inguinal nodes beside the femoral vein, the highest in the femoral canal, and on to the external iliac nodes.
steps.clinical: A lump in the groin may be a node draining an infected toe, a skin cancer of the leg, an anal cancer or a sexually transmitted infection — examine the whole territory.

check.q: Which structure of the male external genitalia does not drain to the superficial inguinal nodes, apart from the testis?
check.a: The glans penis, which drains to the deep inguinal (and external iliac) nodes.

title: How the gut develops
summary: Foregut, midgut and hindgut; rotations and herniation; and the anomalies left behind.
objectives: Define foregut, midgut and hindgut by their arteries and pain referral
Explain how rotation of the stomach produces the lesser sac and the position of the vagal trunks
Describe herniation and rotation of the midgut and the consequences of malrotation
Describe Meckel's diverticulum and the abdominal wall defects
Relate the development of the cloaca to the pectinate line
takeaways: Foregut — coeliac trunk — epigastric pain; midgut — SMA — periumbilical; hindgut — IMA — suprapubic.
The stomach rotates 90° clockwise, so the left vagus becomes anterior and the lesser sac lies behind.
The midgut herniates into the cord and rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA before returning.
Meckel's diverticulum is the persistent vitelline duct on the antimesenteric ileum.
The pectinate line marks the junction of endodermal hindgut and ectodermal proctodeum.

steps.title: Three guts, three arteries
steps.text:
The primitive gut is divided by its blood supply. The foregut — oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum at the major papilla, with the liver, gallbladder and pancreas — is supplied by the coeliac trunk. The midgut — to about two thirds of the way along the transverse colon — by the superior mesenteric artery. The hindgut — to the upper anal canal — by the inferior mesenteric artery.

Visceral pain is felt in the midline at the level of the embryological segment: epigastric, periumbilical and suprapubic respectively.
steps.pitfall: The spleen is supplied by the coeliac trunk but is not a foregut derivative — it develops from mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium.

check.q: Early appendicitis hurts around the umbilicus. Why?
check.a: The appendix is midgut; its visceral afferents enter the cord at T10 with the midgut, and the pain is referred to the periumbilical region until the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

steps.title: The stomach turns
steps.text: The stomach begins as a midline dilation with a dorsal and a ventral mesentery. It rotates 90° clockwise seen from above: the left side faces forward and the right side back. The left vagus therefore ends up anterior and the right posterior. The space created behind the stomach becomes the lesser sac, and the dorsal mesogastrium balloons down as the greater omentum. The spleen develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, leaving the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

check.q: Why is the anterior vagal trunk formed mainly from the left vagus?
check.a: The stomach rotated 90° clockwise, bringing its original left side, with the left vagus, to face forwards.

steps.title: Herniation and rotation of the midgut
steps.text: The midgut grows faster than the abdomen can hold it. In the sixth week it herniates into the umbilical cord as a loop around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. It rotates 270° anticlockwise (seen from the front) in total and returns in the tenth week, jejunum first; the caecum comes back last and descends to the right iliac fossa. The duodenum ends up behind the SMA and the transverse colon in front of it.
steps.clinical: In malrotation, fibrous Ladd bands from a high caecum can also compress the duodenum. Bile in the vomit of a neonate needs urgent contrast study.

check.q: A newborn has bilious vomiting. Why is malrotation an emergency?
check.a: The midgut hangs on a narrow mesenteric base and can twist around the SMA (midgut volvulus), cutting off blood to the whole midgut within hours.

steps.title: The vitelline duct and the abdominal wall
steps.text:
At the apex of the herniated loop the vitelline duct joins the gut to the yolk sac; it normally disappears. If it persists as a pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, it is a Meckel's diverticulum.

If the midgut fails to return, it remains in the cord covered by amnion and peritoneum — an omphalocele, often with other anomalies. A gastroschisis is a full-thickness defect beside the umbilicus, usually on the right, with uncovered bowel.
steps.clinical: Ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid that ulcerates the adjacent ileum, causing painless rectal bleeding in a child; a technetium scan picks up the gastric mucosa.

check.q: State the rule of twos for Meckel's diverticulum.
check.a: About 2% of people, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocaecal valve, about 2 inches long, may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic), and often presents before age 2.

steps.title: The cloaca and the pectinate line
steps.text:
The end of the hindgut opens into the cloaca, which the urorectal septum divides into the rectum behind and the urogenital sinus in front. The anal canal forms where the endodermal hindgut meets an ectodermal pit, the proctodeum, at the pectinate line.

Above the line: columnar epithelium, superior rectal (IMA) supply, portal venous drainage, autonomic nerves, internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes. Below: squamous epithelium, inferior rectal (internal pudendal) supply, systemic veins, somatic pudendal nerve — painful — and superficial inguinal nodes.
steps.clinical: In Hirschsprung disease neural crest cells fail to reach the distal hindgut; the aganglionic rectum cannot relax, and a neonate fails to pass meconium.

check.q: Why are internal haemorrhoids painless and external haemorrhoids painful?
check.a: Internal haemorrhoids arise above the pectinate line, supplied by visceral autonomic nerves; external ones lie below, supplied by the somatic inferior rectal nerves.

steps.title: Liver and pancreas buds
steps.text:
The liver buds from the foregut into the septum transversum, which leaves the ventral mesentery as the lesser omentum and falciform ligament, and the bare area where the liver stays in contact with the diaphragm.

The pancreas forms from a dorsal and a ventral bud. The ventral bud swings round behind the duodenum with the bile duct and fuses with the dorsal bud to form the uncinate process and lower head; the main duct is formed from the ventral duct and the distal dorsal duct.
steps.clinical: If the two ducts fail to fuse (pancreas divisum) most of the gland drains through the small minor papilla, a possible cause of recurrent pancreatitis.

check.q: What is an annular pancreas?
check.a: A ring of pancreatic tissue encircling the second part of the duodenum, from abnormal migration of the ventral bud; it can obstruct the duodenum.

title: How the heart develops
summary: One tube folds and divides into four chambers and two outflows — and each step has its defect.
objectives: Describe the heart tube and looping
Explain atrial septation and the foramen ovale
Explain ventricular septation and why VSDs are usually membranous
Explain outflow tract septation and the conotruncal defects
Describe the fate of the aortic arches and the sinus venosus
takeaways: The primitive heart tube loops to the right, putting the ventricles in front of the atria.
Septum primum and septum secundum overlap as a flap valve: the foramen ovale.
The membranous ventricular septum closes last, from the endocardial cushions — the usual site of a VSD.
A spiral aorticopulmonary septum from neural crest divides the truncus; its errors give TGA, truncus and tetralogy.
The left fourth arch becomes the aortic arch and the left sixth the ductus arteriosus.

steps.title: A tube that loops
steps.text: In the third week paired endocardial tubes fuse into a single heart tube, which begins to beat around day 22. From caudal to cranial it has a sinus venosus, a primitive atrium, a primitive ventricle, the bulbus cordis and the truncus arteriosus. The tube bends to the right (dextral looping), bringing the atrium up behind and the ventricle forward and to the left.
steps.clinical: If looping goes the other way the result is dextrocardia; with complete situs inversus, as in Kartagener syndrome, the heart itself is often otherwise normal.

check.q: What determines that the ventricles lie in front of the atria and the apex points left?
check.a: Rightward (dextral) looping of the primitive heart tube.

steps.title: Dividing the atria
steps.text:
A thin septum primum grows down towards the endocardial cushions, leaving an ostium primum below; before that closes, holes appear in its upper part to form the ostium secundum. A thicker septum secundum then grows down on its right side, leaving an opening — the foramen ovale. The two overlap as a flap valve that lets oxygenated placental blood pass from right to left.

At birth left atrial pressure rises above right, pushing the flap shut; it later fuses, leaving the fossa ovalis.
steps.clinical: The flap fails to fuse in about a quarter of adults — a patent foramen ovale — through which a venous clot can cross to the brain (paradoxical embolism) when right pressure rises. A true ostium secundum defect is the commonest adult ASD.

check.q: What closes the foramen ovale at birth?
check.a: The rise in left atrial pressure (and fall in right) as the lungs expand, pressing septum primum against septum secundum.

steps.title: Dividing the ventricles
steps.text: The muscular interventricular septum grows up from the floor of the ventricle, leaving an interventricular foramen above. That gap is closed by the membranous septum, formed from the endocardial cushions and the conotruncal ridges — the last part of the septum to form.
steps.clinical: A VSD is the commonest congenital heart defect. A small one makes a loud murmur and may close by itself; a large one causes heart failure in infancy and, left alone, pulmonary hypertension with reversal of the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome).

check.q: Why are ventricular septal defects most often in the membranous part?
check.a: It is the last and most complex part to close, requiring fusion of tissue from several sources.

steps.title: Dividing the outflow
steps.text: Neural crest cells migrate into the truncus arteriosus and bulbus cordis and build a spiral aorticopulmonary septum. Because it spirals, the aorta and pulmonary trunk twist around each other as they leave the heart.
steps.clinical: If the septum does not spiral, the great arteries are transposed (TGA) — survival depends on a shunt. If it fails to form, a single persistent truncus arteriosus results. Because neural crest is involved, conotruncal defects go with DiGeorge syndrome.

check.q: Name the four features of tetralogy of Fallot and the single error behind them.
check.a: Pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy — from anterior and superior displacement of the outflow (infundibular) septum.

steps.title: The aortic arches
steps.text: Six pairs of arch arteries appear in sequence, though never all at once. The third arches form the common and proximal internal carotids. The left fourth arch forms part of the aortic arch; the right fourth forms the proximal right subclavian artery. The sixth arches form the proximal pulmonary arteries, and on the left the ductus arteriosus, which becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
steps.clinical: If the right fourth arch regresses abnormally, an aberrant right subclavian artery arises last from the arch and passes behind the oesophagus, sometimes causing dysphagia (dysphagia lusoria).

check.q: Where does coarctation of the aorta usually occur, and what signs does it cause in an adult?
check.a: Just beyond the left subclavian origin, at the ductus; upper limb hypertension, radiofemoral delay and rib notching from enlarged intercostal collaterals.

steps.title: The venous end
steps.text: The right horn of the sinus venosus is absorbed into the right atrium as its smooth-walled part, the sinus venarum, where the venae cavae open; the crista terminalis marks the join with the rough, trabeculated original atrium. The left horn shrinks to become the coronary sinus. On the left, the pulmonary veins are absorbed into the left atrium to form its smooth wall.
steps.clinical: A persistent left superior vena cava drains into a dilated coronary sinus. Atrial fibrillation often starts from sleeves of atrial muscle around the pulmonary vein openings, which is why ablation isolates the pulmonary veins.

check.q: What does the left horn of the sinus venosus become?
check.a: The coronary sinus.

title: Lumbar puncture and neuraxial blocks
summary: Why the needle goes in at L3/4, what it passes through, and what to check before you start.
objectives: Explain why lumbar puncture is performed below L2
Find the L4 spinous process from the iliac crests
List the layers the needle passes through
Distinguish spinal, epidural and caudal anaesthesia
State the contraindications and complications of lumbar puncture
takeaways: The adult cord ends at L1/2; the subarachnoid space and cauda equina continue to S2.
The supracristal (Tuffier's) line crosses the L4 spinous process.
Skin, fat, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura and arachnoid.
Spinal: into CSF. Epidural: stops short of the dura. Caudal: through the sacral hiatus.
Image first if there are signs of raised pressure from a mass; correct coagulopathy.

steps.title: Below the end of the cord
steps.text: In the adult the spinal cord ends at the L1/2 disc (at about L3 in a newborn). Below it the dural sac, full of CSF, continues to S2, containing the roots of the cauda equina, which float away from a needle. A needle at L3/4 or L4/5 therefore enters CSF well below the cord.

check.q: Why is lumbar puncture safe at L3/4 but not at T12?
check.a: At L3/4 the needle enters the dural sac below the end of the cord, among mobile nerve roots; at T12 it would meet the cord.

steps.title: Finding the level
steps.text:
With the patient lying on their side or sitting and curled forward, feel the tops of the iliac crests. A line joining them — the supracristal (Tuffier's) line — crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/5 interspace. Count up one space for L3/4.

Flexing the spine separates the spinous processes and opens the interlaminar window.
steps.pitfall: The supracristal line is only approximate: in obese patients and in pregnancy it often lies a level higher. Ultrasound can confirm the interspace.

check.q: Which spinous process lies on the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests?

steps.title: The layers the needle crosses
steps.text: In the midline the needle passes through skin and subcutaneous fat, the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, and the tough ligamentum flavum — felt as increased resistance and then a give. It is then in the epidural space, full of fat and valveless veins. A further small advance pierces the dura and the arachnoid together, and CSF flows.

check.q: Which ligament gives the characteristic resistance just before the epidural space?
check.a: The ligamentum flavum.

steps.title: Spinal, epidural and caudal
steps.text: A spinal anaesthetic is a small dose placed into the CSF: rapid, dense and predictable, used for caesarean section and lower limb surgery. An epidural uses loss of resistance to stop in the epidural space, where a catheter lets a larger volume be given and topped up: slower, segmental, used in labour. A caudal is an epidural given through the sacral hiatus, commonly in children.
steps.clinical: Leakage of CSF through the dural hole can cause a post-dural puncture headache — worse on standing, eased by lying flat. Fine, pencil-point needles reduce it; an epidural blood patch seals the leak.

check.q: Why does an epidural need a much larger dose than a spinal anaesthetic?
check.a: The drug has to diffuse through the dura to the roots from outside, and spreads through a larger space, whereas a spinal places it directly in the CSF bathing the roots.

steps.title: When not to do it
steps.text: Removing CSF from below when a mass lesion is raising pressure above can pull the brain down through the tentorium or foramen magnum — coning. Signs of raised pressure, a focal deficit, papilloedema or a reduced conscious level call for a CT scan first. A bleeding tendency or anticoagulation risks an epidural haematoma compressing the cauda equina, and infected skin at the site risks meningitis or an epidural abscess.
steps.clinical: New back pain, leg weakness or bladder disturbance after a neuraxial block or puncture in an anticoagulated patient is an epidural haematoma until proved otherwise — urgent MRI.

check.q: Why is a CT head done before lumbar puncture in a drowsy patient with a focal deficit?
check.a: To exclude a mass lesion with raised pressure, where lowering CSF pressure from below could cause herniation (coning).
